parent.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation
parent.overview: 1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 is a crossroads, not one system: White develops the b1-knight before committing the c-pawn, which blocks White's own c-pawn and so gives up the usual c4 challenge to d5. The usual continuation is 2...Nf6, after which White chooses between 3.Bg5 (Richter-Veresov: pin on f6, queenside castling, f3 and e4) and 3.Bf4 (Jobava London: Nb5 ideas against c7, Qd2 and Bh6 against a fianchetto), or 3.Nf3 and transpositions. Other Black replies are 2...Bf5 (Alburt Defence, assessed as equal, rare in master play), 2...c5 (Irish Gambit, little explored) and 2...e6. The openings are rarely used by top players as a main weapon but are sound; Spassky, Tal, Karpov, Bronstein, Morozevich, Aronian and Gashimov have played them as surprise weapons. The subtree also swallows a different opening by transposition: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nc6 is the Chigorin Defence, Black's choice, not White's.

parent.name: Bird Opening
parent.overview: 1.f4 stakes a claim to e5 and gives White attacking chances at the cost of slightly weakening the kingside (the h4-e1 diagonal). Black's most common reply is 1...d5, which gives a reversed Dutch Defence with White a tempo up, and White chooses between a reversed Leningrad (Nf3, g3, Bg2, O-O), a Stonewall (pawns on d4, e3, f4, with a kingside pawn storm) or a queenside fianchetto to hold e5. Black's sharpest answer is 1...e5, From's Gambit, which is notoriously double-edged and shows the Qh4+ danger. Other replies include 1...Nf6, 1...c5 and 1...b6. White scores below 50% (about 47%), and the opening is rare at the very top, but it is a respectable surprise weapon (Larsen, Bird).

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: French Variation
parent.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6
parent.overview: 2...e6 is a gateway rather than a set-up: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black chooses the Taimanov (...Nc6), the Kan (...a6) or the Scheveningen (...d6, ...Nf6), with 3.Nc3 giving the Paulsen/Kan/Taimanov move orders. Black opens the diagonal for the f8-bishop and prepares ...d5 or ...Nc6/...a6 in a flexible way, with a solid ...e6/...d6 pawn chain and queenside counterplay. The name 'French' is only a naming convention: the pawn structure is Sicilian, not a French one. White's main choice is 3.d4 (about 61% of moves at 2500); rarer third moves are 3.d3, 3.g3, 3.c3 and Westerinen's 3.b3 (Bb2, occasional in the 1970s). At higher levels play is heavily theoretical.

parent.name: King's Indian Attack
parent.overview: White builds the mirror image of the King's Indian Defence: Nf3, g3, Bg2, O-O, d3, Nbd2 and e4, usually against any Black set-up, particularly ...d5 with ...e6 or ...c5. The central pawn push e4-e5 gives a kingside bind and space, after which White expands with h4-h5, g4 and knight manoeuvres (Nf1-e3/g3 or Ne1-g2) towards a kingside attack. Black generally seeks counterplay on the queenside with ...c5, ...b5 or ...a5, or contests e4 directly. It has a modest theory load and keeps the same ideas whatever Black plays, so it is popular at club level, though it is uncommon among top grandmasters today. Black's main dilemma is that passive play lets White have a superior version of the King's Indian Defence, while ...e5 can leave Black behind in development.

parent.name: King's Indian Defense
parent.overview: Black fianchettoes the dark-squared bishop, castles and lets White build a big pawn centre (c4, d4, e4), then attacks it with ...e5 or ...c5 while preparing kingside play. In the main Classical/Mar del Plata structure the centre locks after d5 and the game becomes a race: White expands on the queenside with c4-c5 while Black storms the kingside with ...f5-f4 and ...g5. Other White systems change the picture: Samisch (f3) is aggressive with opposite-side castling attacks, Four Pawns (f4) maximises space, Averbakh (Bg5) keeps ...e5 in check, and the Fianchetto (g3) is quieter and positional. Sources describe it as dynamic, exceptionally complex and moderately risky for both sides, with a heavy theory burden because White has many fifth-move systems. Considered sound today after being held suspect until the 1930s.

parent.name: Pirc Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 d6 2. d4 Nf6 3. Nc3 g6
parent.overview: Black plays 1...d6 and, after 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3, ...g6 and ...Bg7, letting White build the broad e4-d4 centre and then undermining it from the flanks with ...c5 or ...e5 (hypermodern: the bigger White's centre, the bigger the target). The root is a crossroads: 1...d6 can transpose to the Philidor (3...e5 or ...c6) or to the Modern. White's replies run from sharp (Austrian Attack 4.f4, 150 Attack 4.Be3 with Qd2, Bh6 and h4-h5, Byrne 4.Bg5, Bayonet h4) to unhurried (Classical 4.Nf3 with Be2 and castling, fianchetto). Typical play is imbalanced: White gets space and often a kingside attack, Black gets a solid fianchettoed king and counterplay on the queenside and with central breaks. It is sound but has a reputation for giving White chances; Kasparov doubted it for the top level (s1), though Caruana, Anand and Grischuk have used it (s2).

parent.name: Dutch Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...f5, fighting for e4 and avoiding symmetrical play, at the cost of weakening the kingside (the e8-h5 diagonal) and the e6 square. Three set-ups dominate: the Leningrad (...g6, ...Bg7, KID-style, with ...e5 or ...Ne4 and kingside play), the Stonewall (...e6, ...d5, ...c6 with a knight on e4 and a bad light-squared bishop) and the Classical (...e6, ...Be7, ...d6, later ...e5). White usually fianchettoes with g3/Bg2 and c4 and prepares e4 or queenside expansion, or sidesteps theory with the Staunton Gambit (2.e4), Hopton or Korchnoi Attack (h3 and g4). Sources agree it is sound but double-edged, unbalancing and theoretical, played occasionally by Carlsen, Nakamura and Nepomniachtchi but never a main defence to 1.d4.

parent.name: Modern Defense
parent.overview: Black plays 1...g6 and 2...Bg7 and lets White build the e4-d4 centre, delaying ...Nf6 (which separates it from the Pirc), then attacks the centre with ...c5, ...e5 or ...Nc6 and the pressure of the g7 bishop. It is a simple, repeatable set-up that Black can adopt against almost anything, and its flexible move order makes it a practical surprise weapon. White's main tries are the Standard line (2.d4 Bg7 3.Nc3 d6 4.f4 or 3.Nf3), the Averbakh-style 2.c4 / 2.Nc3 set-ups, and c3 to blunt the g7 bishop; White often attacks on the kingside with f4, while Black seeks counterplay against an over-extended centre. Sources call it sound but with a risk of passivity or of letting White build an overwhelming centre; it is moderately popular (about 1.7% of games in 2025 on one database) with occasional master use (Suttles, Davies, McNab, Carlsen).

parent.name: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation
parent.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 g6 3. Nc3 Bg7 4. e4 d6
parent.overview: This root is the King's Indian reached by the move order 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.c4 (the same position as 3.Nf3 in the 2.c4 move order). It is not a distinct opening: it is the ordinary King's Indian, where Black fianchettoes with ...Bg7, castles, and strikes at White's centre with ...e5, ...c5 or ...f5. White's choice of set-up decides the character: the classical 4.Nc3 and e4 leads to the locked-centre opposite-wing race (c4-c5 against ...f5-f4), while the Fianchetto Variation (g3, Bg2, O-O, Nc3) is quieter, positional, and has less forcing theory. The data subtree groups 4.e4 Normal Variation lines (the majority of games) under this root, so it mixes both. Black's success depends on timing and coordination rather than automatic aggression.

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Declined
parent.overview: Black meets 2.c4 with 2...e6, holding d5 and keeping a secure, compact centre rather than taking the pawn. It is one of Black's most reliable defences to 1.d4 (s1). The price is the light-squared bishop on c8, which is shut in behind the e6-pawn and is Black's main strategic problem (s1). The game then usually becomes a manoeuvring fight: White uses the minority attack (b4-b5) in Carlsbad structures or central expansion with e4 or e4-e5 (Botvinnik plan), while Black aims for the freeing ...c5 or ...e5 break, a Lasker-style exchange of pieces, or a bishop fianchetto (s1, s2, s3). Both Wikipedia and Chessable stress that it is extremely sound yet can turn double-edged when both sides pursue their plans (s2). It was the staple of the Alekhine-Capablanca match (s1) and is played from beginner level to world champions (s2).

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
parent.overview: After 2...dxc4 Black has taken the c-pawn, but sources agree he cannot keep it without serious concessions; White regains it with Bxc4 once the e-pawn has moved (3.e3 or 3.Nf3 then e3, or 3.e4). Black instead gives up the idea of holding it and fights for central counterplay: ...c5 (and ...cxd4) or ...e5 to undermine d4, and ...a6 with ...b5 to gain queenside space and time for the c8 bishop. The centre is open, White has the d4/e4 pawns and the move, and the usual middlegames are IQP or hanging-pawn positions with piece play. Character varies by line: the 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Bxc4 c5 main line is positional and balanced, while 3.e4 lines can be tactical early. It is sound and has been a regular at the elite level since the 1990s.
